prime.problem: You can now get exact gradients for any expression, but an expression that just sits there learns nothing. To make a net fit data you need a way to build many neurons at once, one number that says how wrong they are, and a repeatable step that makes that number smaller.
prime.fits: This is the payoff of the whole lecture. The single neuron and the automatic backward() from earlier cards become the building blocks; the one manual nudge from the one-step card becomes a loop that runs itself.
prime.goal: Write an MLP from scratch, train it on four examples until the loss is below 0.02, and explain why every line of the loop, especially the gradient reset, has to be there.

attend: Where do the 41 parameters come from, and why does each neuron contribute one more than its number of inputs?
Why does squaring the miss make the two wrong-sign predictions dominate the starting loss of 6.0054?
Why is the update p.data += -lr * p.grad and not + lr * p.grad?
Since += was the fix on the accumulate-gradients card, why does it become a bug across training steps?
How can the loop that forgets zero_grad end with a lower loss and still be wrong?

must: Neuron = tanh(w·x + b) → a Layer is independent neurons sharing one input → an MLP chains layers → the whole net is one big Value expression → one loss.backward() reaches all 41 parameters

Loss = sum of squared misses → one number that is 0 only when every prediction hits its target → its gradient with respect to each parameter says which way that knob raises the loss → stepping by -lr × grad lowers it

_backward adds into .grad (needed for reused nodes) → without a reset, step k uses the sum of all earlier gradients → an ever-growing, stale step size → loss can jump (0.000311 → 0.174190 at step 7) or diverge; on this easy problem it hides
lr sets the step length → too small crawls (lr 0.01: 2.5453 after 20 steps) → too big overshoots and can saturate tanh (lr 0.5: stuck at 3.9999) → you pick it by watching the loss
elevated: tanh on the output neuron too → predictions are trapped in (−1, 1) → fine here because the targets are ±1, but a saturated output has almost no gradient, which is how lr 0.5 gets stuck
reference: random.uniform(-1, 1) init and random.seed(1337) (the lab's seed, taken from micrograd's demo.ipynb)
sum(..., self.b) uses the bias as the start value of the sum
Layer returns outs[0] when it has a single neuron
micrograd's nn.py: ReLU, bias 0, linear last layer, Module.zero_grad()
the exact printed digits (they can vary in the last place)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the training loop as a cycle of four boxes and write under each box the one line of code it runs. Then, in 2–3 sentences, say what goes wrong if you delete the reset box.
checklist: forward: run the net on every example and compute the loss
backward: loss.backward() fills a fresh gradient into all 41 parameters
update: p.data += -lr * p.grad, with the minus because the gradient points uphill
no reset → gradients from earlier steps pile up → a stale, growing step that can overshoot

retrieve.q: Explain why the loss for this net is a single number, and what property of squaring makes it a sensible thing to minimise.
answer: backward needs one output node to start from (grad 1.0)
squaring makes every miss positive, so misses can't cancel
it's 0 only when all four predictions equal their targets
big misses count much more: the two wrong-sign examples give 5.38 of the 6.01

retrieve.q: Count the parameters of MLP(3, [4, 4, 1]) layer by layer, without looking.
answer: each neuron has one weight per input plus one bias
output: 1 × (4 + 1) = 5, total 41

retrieve.q: Walk through one pass of the loop for the weight layers[0].neurons[0].w[0]: what is its grad after backward at step 0, and what is its new value?
answer: grad −0.4537 after loss.backward()
negative grad means raising this weight lowers the loss, and the step raises it

retrieve.q: You're choosing a learning rate for this net. What does each of 0.01 and 0.5 cost you, and how would you tell from the printed losses which mistake you've made?
answer: 0.01: steady but slow, loss still 2.5453 after 20 steps
0.5: overshoots, a tanh saturates and the loss freezes at 3.9999
slow and steady decrease → raise lr; jumps up or a flat plateau at a high value → lower it

compare.q: That card moved the leaves along the gradient once to raise L; this card moves parameters against it twenty times to lower the loss. What changed about the goal, what stays identical in the mechanism, and why does the loop need a reset that the one-step card never did?
answer: same mechanism: nudge each number by a small multiple of its own gradient
goal flipped: raise L there, lower the loss here, hence the minus sign
one step there, a loop here that recomputes the forward pass every time
the reset matters only when backward runs more than once on the same parameters

compare.q: The neural bigram model trains with the same four-move loop but on tensors and with a different loss. What carries over unchanged, what is swapped out, and what would break first if you tried to train it with micrograd's scalar Values?
answer: unchanged: forward, zero the grads, backward, update with -lr × grad
swapped: squared error becomes negative log likelihood; scalars become tensors
PyTorch uses p.grad = None for the reset, same purpose
scalar Values would break on speed: one Python object per number, for tens of thousands of examples

predict.q: Someone moves the reset so it runs after loss.backward() and before the update. Same seed, lr 0.1. What loss does the loop print at steps 0, 1 and 2?
predict.answer: 6.005402783252284 every time. The reset wipes the fresh gradients right before the update reads them, so every step adds −0.1 × 0 and no parameter ever moves. Order matters: the reset belongs before backward().

apply.task: Add an lr sweep to your loop (or run the lab's train(True, lr=..., verbose=False)) for lr = 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5, all with random.seed(1337), and record the loss at step 19. Then, for the worst one, print the final predictions and explain what went wrong.
apply.done: Your step-19 losses are about 2.5453, 0.0596, 0.0178, 0.0001 and 3.9999, and you can explain the last one: its final predictions are about [1.0, −0.9997, 1.0, 1.0], so the third example (target −1) is stuck at +1 with a saturated tanh and almost no gradient to pull it back.
apply.hint: Print the whole loss list for lr 0.2 too: it reaches 0.0001, but only after bouncing up to 4.6405 at step 5. Big steps can land well by luck.
